n: After David speaks with Saul, Jonathan's soul is “knit” to David's — a deep, loyal friendship. Jonathan, the heir to the throne, loves the man who will replace him, without jealousy.

f.w: loved him as his own soul

n: Saul keeps David at court permanently instead of letting him return home.
Jonathan and David make a covenant — a sacred, binding promise of loyalty to each other and their families.
Jonathan gives David his robe, armor, sword, bow, and belt. Symbolically, the crown prince hands over his royal identity and status to David.

f.g: belt, often used to hold weapons

n: David succeeds in every mission Saul gives him and acts wisely. Saul promotes him over the soldiers, and everyone — even Saul's officials — approves.

f.g: The Hebrew also implies success; wisdom and success go together for David here.

n: As the army returns from battle, women from all Israel's towns come out singing and dancing with tambourines and instruments to greet the king — a traditional victory celebration.
Their song: “Saul has killed his thousands, and David his ten thousands.” In Hebrew poetry this may simply honor both, but Saul hears it as a comparison.

f.w: Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands

n: Saul becomes furious and jealous. He fears that David, now more praised than he, will soon take the kingdom too.

f.w: what can he have more but the kingdom?

n: From that day Saul keeps a suspicious, jealous eye on David. Envy begins to consume him.
The next day the troubling spirit comes on Saul, and he raves in the house while David plays music as usual. Saul has a spear in his hand.

f.g: Here it describes frenzied, uncontrolled raving rather than true prophecy.
JST: “the evil spirit which was not of God.”

n: Saul hurls the spear, trying to pin David to the wall. David dodges it twice. Jealousy has turned to murderous rage.
Saul is afraid of David because the Lord is with David and has left Saul.
Saul sends David away from court as commander of a thousand men — perhaps hoping he would be killed. But this gives David even more public exposure.

f.w: went out and came in before the people
f.g: led the people, especially in military campaigns

n: David continues to act wisely and succeed in everything, because the Lord is with him.
David's success only makes Saul more afraid of him.
Meanwhile, all Israel and Judah love David because he leads them in battle. The people's hearts are turning to him.
Saul offers his oldest daughter Merab in marriage if David will keep fighting the Lord's battles. Secretly he hopes the Philistines will kill David so his own hands stay clean.

f.w: Let not mine hand be upon him

n: David humbly asks who he is, or his family, to become the king's son-in-law.
When the time comes, Saul breaks his promise and gives Merab to another man, Adriel. This is a public insult to David.
Saul's younger daughter Michal loves David. When Saul hears, he is pleased — but for the wrong reasons.
Saul plans to use Michal as a trap to get David killed by the Philistines. He tells David he will have a second chance to become his son-in-law.

f.w: in the one of the twain
f.g: through the second of the two daughters

n: Saul has his servants secretly encourage David, flattering him that the king and everyone love him and want him as son-in-law.
David replies that he is a poor man of low standing — how could he afford to marry the king's daughter? A bride-price was expected.
The servants report David's response to Saul.
Saul names an unusual bride-price: proof of one hundred dead Philistines. It sounds like honor, but he hopes David will die trying.

f.g: bride-price paid to the bride's father
Proof that the dead were uncircumcised Philistines, not Israelites.

n: David is pleased with the offer and acts quickly, before the deadline expires.

f.g: the time limit had not yet run out

n: David and his men kill two hundred Philistines — double the price — and present the proof in full. Saul has no choice but to give him Michal.

f.g: in full number, counted out completely

n: Saul realizes that the Lord is with David and that his own daughter loves him. Every plan to harm David has backfired.
Saul grows even more afraid and becomes David's lifelong enemy.
Whenever the Philistine commanders came out to fight, David was more successful than all Saul's other officers, and his name became highly honored.
